extraction.name: MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI
extraction.description: A benchmark of 11.5K carefully selected college-level multimodal questions from exams, quizzes, textbooks, online sources, and lecture materials, covering 30 subjects, 183 subfields, six disciplines, and 30 image types to evaluate multimodal understanding and reasoning.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen
extraction.citeAs: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen. MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI. arXiv:2311.16502.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark collection takes three stages. First, the authors went through common university majors to decide which subjects to include, selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on whether visual inputs are commonly adopted. Second, they recruited over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources and to create new questions based on their expertise where necessary. This resulted in a diverse collection of 13K questions from various sources. Third, the authors performed quality control including duplicate detection, format and typo checking, and difficulty categorization, excluding approximately 10% of problems classified as very easy. The final benchmark contains 11.5K questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Others
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions were sourced from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, online sources, lecture materials, free online resources, and other study materials.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Potential duplicate problems were identified using lexical overlap and source URL similarity and then reviewed by the authors to eliminate duplications. Problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking. Authors categorized problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of problems classified as very easy were excluded from the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were standardized into a structured JSON format including fields for question type, question text, answer options for multiple-choice questions, correct answer, question difficulty, and explanation if available. Images were inserted as file paths in the question, options, or explanations. All questions were required to contain one or more images, be written in English, meet college-level difficulty, be unambiguous, and be answerable with one of the given options or a short answer.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the selected majors served as annotators to collect multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources and create new questions where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoid sources prohibiting copying or redistribution, and select questions whose answers were not immediately available to reduce contamination. The annotation protocol required annotating all fields including question, answer options for multiple-choice questions, correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation if available. Questions had to contain one or more images, be in English, be college-level, and be unambiguous. Ambiguous instances were flagged for detailed review and discussed in team meetings.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A user-friendly web interface for data annotation and verification
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A secondary review team rigorously vetted annotations for quality and guideline adherence. Regular audits of random samples were conducted to ensure sustained quality and consistency. Ambiguous or unclear instances were flagged for detailed review and collaboratively examined in team meetings to establish a standardized approach for annotation.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the selected majors and various disciplines and subjects; 50 college students are also described as collecting questions, and 90 college senior students were involved as human experts for evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The appendix includes a version change log. Changes are documented from V1 (Nov.27) to V2 (Dec.18), V3 (Dec.21), and V4 (June.13). Xiang Yue took the lead in the dataset release. The benchmark also has a live-updating leaderboard on the project website.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes questions from Health & Medicine and Public Health and may involve sensitive domains such as medical images and pathology. The annotation protocol explicitly instructs annotators to avoid collecting questions that contain any private information.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that monitoring progress toward Expert AGI is of intellectual and societal importance because Expert AGI could lead to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. The authors believe MMMU will be instrumental in developing next-generation multimodal foundation models and monitoring progress towards Expert AGI.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper states that MMMU, like any benchmark, has limitations and that the manual curation process may carry biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper cautions that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and the 90th percentile of skilled adults, nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. It also states that the manual curation process may carry biases and that the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed as a benchmark to evaluate multimodal models on college-level multi-discipline multimodal understanding and reasoning. It is divided into a few-shot development set, a validation set useful for hyperparameter selection, and a test set. The authors evaluate models in zero-shot settings and also report few-shot results for selected models in the appendix.
